bottleneck: Silencing genes in the central nervous system requires crossing the blood-brain barrier or invasive intrathecal delivery, and distribution through brain parenchyma is uneven — deep structures receive far less drug than cortical surfaces. Antisense and siRNA approaches for Huntington's and ALS have shown target lowering without clear clinical benefit, suggesting that timing, brain-region coverage, and which cell types are silenced matter as much as the knockdown itself. Partial, patchy silencing may be worse than none if it creates false confidence.
current_state: Intrathecal antisense drugs are approved for SMA and in trials for Huntington's and ALS, but CNS-wide, even distribution remains unsolved. Delivery science lags the oligonucleotide chemistry.

sources.title: Architecting the Future of Health: From Code to Cure

title: Gene silencing cannot distribute evenly in the brain
why_it_blocks: Neurodegeneration is a whole-brain problem; silencing that reaches only patches of it cannot halt disease. Uneven CNS distribution caps the ceiling of every brain gene-silencing program, no matter how potent the molecule.
